description: Believes DISTINCT applies only to the first column after it (or to each column separately), instead of removing rows whose whole combination of selected columns repeats
example_wrong_answer: SELECT DISTINCT customer, city gives one row per customer, because the DISTINCT is on customer.

description: Believes DISTINCT reduces a column to a single value, keeping the first row it finds, rather than keeping every different value
example_wrong_answer: If I put DISTINCT on the price I get just one price back, the first one it finds.
source: Adapted from Miedema, Aivaloglou & Fletcher, ICER 2021 (DISTINCT believed to take the first item)

description: Believes AND and OR in a WHERE clause have equal priority and are applied left to right, not knowing that AND is evaluated before OR
example_wrong_answer: dept = 'IT' OR dept = 'HR' AND salary > 50000 gives the IT and HR people who earn more than 50000.

description: Believes col = NULL (or col <> NULL) tests whether a value is missing, the same way IS NULL / IS NOT NULL does
example_wrong_answer: WHERE city = NULL returns the customers whose city is missing.
source: Adapted from Miedema, Aivaloglou & Fletcher, ICER 2021 (confusing IS / IS NOT with the = / <> comparison operators)

description: Believes a row whose column is NULL satisfies col <> 'x', because a missing value is 'not equal' to 'x'
example_wrong_answer: Ben has no city, so city <> 'Pune' is true for him and he is returned.

description: Believes SUM and AVG treat NULL as 0, so AVG divides by the number of all rows including those with NULL
example_wrong_answer: The bonuses are 100, 200, 300 and two NULLs, so the average is 600 / 5 = 120.

description: Believes x NOT IN (subquery) works normally even when the subquery returns a NULL, not realising the condition can then never be true
example_wrong_answer: Ben's id 2 is not in the list (1, 3, NULL), so NOT IN returns Ben; the NULL in the list doesn't matter.

description: Believes LEFT JOIN drops left-table rows that have no match, like INNER JOIN
example_wrong_answer: Ben has no orders, so he won't appear in the result.

description: Believes a join returns at most one row per row of the left table, rather than one row for every matching pair
example_wrong_answer: Asha is one customer, so she appears once in the join even though she has two orders.

description: Believes that listing two tables in FROM without a join condition makes the database match rows on their related key automatically, instead of producing every combination of rows
example_wrong_answer: FROM customers, orders already links each order to its own customer because both tables have the customer id.
source: Adapted from Miedema, Aivaloglou & Fletcher, ICER 2021 (DBMS treated as a black box; missing join condition)

description: Believes a WHERE condition on a right-table column after a LEFT JOIN still keeps the unmatched left rows, not realising it removes the NULL-extended rows and makes the query behave like an inner join
example_wrong_answer: It's a LEFT JOIN, so Ben is still listed with NULL; WHERE o.status = 'paid' only removes the unpaid orders.

description: Believes COUNT(column) counts every row, including rows where that column is NULL, exactly like COUNT(*)
example_wrong_answer: COUNT(bonus) is 5 because there are five staff rows.

description: Believes conditions on aggregates (such as COUNT(*) >= 2) can go in WHERE, treating WHERE and HAVING as interchangeable, not realising WHERE filters individual rows before any grouping
example_wrong_answer: You can just write WHERE COUNT(*) >= 2; WHERE and HAVING both filter, so it is the same thing.
source: Adapted from Miedema, Aivaloglou & Fletcher, ICER 2021 (aggregates used in the WHERE clause)

description: Believes GROUP BY only sorts or clusters rows and keeps every row, so adding it to a query cannot change the number of rows returned
example_wrong_answer: GROUP BY city just puts the stores of the same city next to each other; all the stores are still listed.
source: Adapted from Miedema, Aivaloglou & Fletcher, ICER 2021 (believing an added GROUP BY 'can't hurt' an ordering query)

description: Believes that counting the column you grouped by (GROUP BY city with COUNT(city)) always gives 1 per group, because each group contains only one distinct city
example_wrong_answer: COUNT(city) will be 1 for every row, since each group has just one city in it.
source: Adapted from Miedema, Aivaloglou & Fletcher, ICER 2021 (counting the column that is grouped on)

description: Believes that defining a CTE with WITH changes the result even when the main query never references it, as if the CTE filtered the underlying table
example_wrong_answer: The WITH clause already removed the NULL customer ids, so the main query no longer sees them.
source: Adapted from Miedema, Aivaloglou & Fletcher, ICER 2021 (defining a WITH query but not using it in the main query)

description: Believes a correlated subquery is evaluated once for the whole query and gives the same value on every outer row, rather than being re-evaluated for each outer row
example_wrong_answer: The subquery counts the orders once, so every customer gets the same number, the total number of orders.

description: Believes WHERE id IN (subquery) returns an outer row once for every matching subquery row, like a join, so duplicates in the subquery duplicate the output
example_wrong_answer: Asha has three orders, so she appears three times in the result of the IN query.

description: Believes window functions collapse rows into one per partition like GROUP BY, rather than keeping every input row and adding a computed column
example_wrong_answer: SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id) returns one row per customer with their total.

description: Believes ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK treat tied rows the same way (for example that RANK never leaves gaps, or that ROW_NUMBER gives tied rows the same number)
example_wrong_answer: Asha and Ben both earn 90000, so they both get 1 and Chen gets 2 in all three columns.

description: Believes SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY y) returns the grand total on every row, not knowing that ORDER BY inside OVER produces a running total in which tied rows share a value
example_wrong_answer: The ORDER BY only sorts the rows, so every row shows the overall total of 200.

description: Believes adding an index always makes the database faster with no downside, ignoring the extra storage, the slower INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE, and that the planner may not use it
example_wrong_answer: Just put an index on every column; indexes only make things faster.

description: Believes a composite index on (a, b) speeds up a query that filters only on b just as well as one that filters on a
example_wrong_answer: There is an index on (last_name, first_name), so searching by first_name alone is fast too.

description: Believes a plain index on a column is still used when the WHERE clause wraps that column in a function or expression, such as LOWER(email) or extracting the year from a date
example_wrong_answer: created_at is indexed, so filtering on the year of created_at uses the index.

description: Believes primary-key values can repeat in a table, so DISTINCT is needed when selecting the primary-key column
example_wrong_answer: I'd write SELECT DISTINCT id FROM customers to be safe, in case an id appears twice.
source: Adapted from Miedema, Aivaloglou & Fletcher, ICER 2021 (uncertainty about primary keys; DISTINCT applied to key columns)

description: Believes a foreign-key column must hold unique values like a primary key, so the same parent row cannot be referenced by several child rows
example_wrong_answer: orders.customer_id is a foreign key, so each customer id can appear only once in orders.

description: Believes normalisation is only about saving disk space, missing that repeated copies of a fact can become inconsistent when only some of them are updated (update anomalies)
example_wrong_answer: Repeating the city on every order just wastes a bit of space; otherwise it is harmless.

description: Believes that when a later statement in a transaction fails and the transaction is rolled back, the earlier statements stay saved (ROLLBACK only undoes the last statement)
example_wrong_answer: The first update already ran, so A has lost the 100 even though the transaction was rolled back.

description: Believes other sessions see a transaction's changes as soon as each statement runs, before COMMIT
example_wrong_answer: Right after the first UPDATE, anyone querying account A sees the reduced balance.

description: Believes that wrapping statements in a transaction at the default isolation level (such as READ COMMITTED) makes concurrent transactions behave as if they ran one after another, so lost updates and non-repeatable reads cannot happen
example_wrong_answer: Both decrements are inside transactions, so they can't interfere and the stock ends at 8.
